analysis.one_liner: Requires larger helicopters to carry flight recorders, cockpit voice recorders, and terrain warning systems.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee markup, a floor vote, or a single vote of any kind; it died with the 116th Congress on January 3, 2021, with 4 House sponsors and no committee action after its first day.
analysis.plain_summary: After the January 2020 helicopter crash near Calabasas, California, that killed Kobe Bryant, his daughter Gianna, and seven others, this bill would have ordered the FAA to require helicopters with six or more passenger seats to carry a flight data recorder, a cockpit voice recorder, and a terrain awareness and warning system. It would have implemented safety recommendations the National Transportation Safety Board first made in 2006 that the FAA had not acted on. Operators would have had one to two years to install the equipment.
analysis.who_benefits: Passengers on larger helicopters — charter customers, tour groups, and corporate riders — and their families. Terrain warning systems help pilots avoid flying into hills or terrain they cannot see in fog or darkness, and the recorders give investigators the data needed to determine why a crash happened. The bill's findings point to crashes like the 2004 Gulf of Mexico helicopter crash that killed 10 people and a 2011 Missouri crash that killed 4 as the kind of accidents the equipment addresses.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Helicopter passengers and crash victims' families

how_it_helps.text: Requires all U.S.-registered turbine-powered helicopters certificated for six or more passenger seats to be equipped with a flight data recorder, a cockpit voice recorder, and a terrain awareness and warning system, with compliance due one to two years after the FAA issues its rules.

Forces the FAA to implement long-standing NTSB safety recommendations it had not acted on, including the 2006 recommendation to close exemption loopholes that let transport-category helicopters fly without flight recorders.

Terrain awareness and warning systems alert pilots when they are on a path toward terrain — the type of controlled-flight-into-terrain risk the NTSB has repeatedly flagged in fatal helicopter crashes; the bill's findings cite a 2004 Gulf of Mexico crash that killed 10 and a 2011 Missouri crash that killed 4.

analysis.who_pays: Owners and operators of larger turbine helicopters — charter companies, tour operators, and corporate fleets — who would have to buy and install the recorders and warning system within one to two years. Those costs would largely flow through to charter and tour prices. The FAA would also bear the work of writing the regulations within 90 days.
analysis.who_pays_short: Helicopter operators, passed to charter customers

drawbacks.text: The retrofit requirement would impose real equipment and installation costs on operators of existing six-plus-seat helicopters, with a compliance window of only one to two years after the rules are issued — a cost that would be passed on to charter and tour customers.

The bill lets the FAA exempt any civilian helicopter from one or more of the equipment requirements, which could hollow out the mandate; the bill's own findings criticize existing FAA exemptions, yet the exemption power remains, and operators would only be entitled to a report to Congress explaining any exemption after the fact.

The scope is narrow: it covers only turbine-powered helicopters certificated for six or more passenger seats, leaving smaller helicopters — which make up much of the fleet and are involved in many crashes — entirely untouched.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — giving pilots terrain warnings and giving investigators the data to determine crash causes on larger passenger helicopters — is real and modest in cost, since it applies only to the larger end of the fleet. The design is reasonable but imperfect: the FAA's broad exemption authority could undercut the mandate, and small helicopters, where many accidents occur, are left out. Weighed honestly, this was a targeted, low-cost safety bill rather than a sweeping one.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee on the day it was introduced and to its Aviation Subcommittee the next day, and no one ever brought it up for a committee vote or a floor vote before the term ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Brad Sherman introduced the bill on June 18, 2020, naming it for Kobe Bryant and his daughter Gianna, who were among the nine people killed in the January 26, 2020 helicopter crash near Calabasas, California.

The bill's findings state that the helicopter in the Calabasas crash had no flight data recorder, no cockpit voice recorder, and no terrain awareness and warning system, and that the FAA had not acted on several NTSB recommendations for helicopter safety equipment.

The bill was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee on June 18, 2020, and to that committee's Aviation Subcommittee on June 19, 2020; no further action of any kind was taken.
Three Democrats — Reps. Juan Vargas, Mark Takano, and Ed Case — cosponsored the bill, and no vote was ever held before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Operators of larger helicopters are better off because the bill died — they avoid mandatory recorder and terrain-warning retrofits — and the FAA avoids a statutory 90-day deadline to write the rules; helicopter passengers gained no new protections.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors were Democrats and no Republicans signed on, but no vote was ever taken and no member's opposition appears anywhere in the record, so the partisan shape of the bill was never tested.

industries.industry: Helicopter charter, tour, and corporate operators (turbine aircraft, 6+ seats)
industries.note: Operators of larger helicopters would have had to buy and install flight data recorders, cockpit voice recorders, and terrain awareness and warning systems within one to two years, and the bill's findings document that many aircraft flying passengers today lack this equipment. The industry avoided this cost when the bill died; passengers kept flying on unequipped aircraft.

industries.industry: Avionics manufacturers (flight recorders and terrain warning systems)
industries.note: A mandate covering all six-plus-seat U.S.-registered turbine helicopters would have created a guaranteed market for crash-resistant recorders and terrain awareness systems. The industry's interest ran alongside passenger safety here.
